2023_065_5_e_people_driven_technology_00.paragraph: Quote #003867, version 1, issued by People Driven Technology, Inc. (East Michigan office) to the Troy School District and carried as agenda item 5.E. on the March 21, 2023 Board of Education agenda. The quote prices 50 Dell Latitude 3420 laptops, part number PDT-LAT3420, at $676.00 each for an extended price of $33,800.00, which is also the subtotal and the quote total. Pricing is drawn from Midwestern Higher Education Compact (MHEC) contract code C000000978628. The document is dated 02/08/2023 with a delivery date of 02/08/2023 and an expiration date of 03/10/2023.

2023_066_5_d_pilot_classroom_furniture_d.paragraph: A February 8, 2023 furniture selection packet prepared for the Troy School District and presented as agenda item 5.D. on March 21, 2023, defining the pilot classroom furniture design kits available for selection. It organizes offerings into seven families, single student tables, two-top and four-top student tables, group set-ups, teacher furniture, ancillary seating, and storage, each specified by manufacturer, dimensions, height range, mobility option and quantity. Color and finish preferences were to be gathered at Workshop #2 and factored into final selections with the Executive team, and furniture is to be sized by grade level.
2023_066_5_d_pilot_classroom_furniture_d.page:
Purpose and Process
Prepared for the Troy School District and dated February 8, 2023, the packet presents 'Pilot Classroom Furniture Design Kits' for staff selection. Input on furniture colors and finishes will be gathered at Workshop #2 and factored into final color selections with the Executive team, and the professional and executive teams will size furniture by grade level. Typical height bands listed are Pre-K, Pre-K to K, K to 2nd, 3rd to 5th, 3rd to 12th, and 9th to 12th.

Kit Families
| Series | Category | Kits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Single Student Table | 1a, 1b, 1c |
| 2 | Student Table - Two Top | 2a, 2b, 2c |
| 3 | Student Table - Four Top | 3a, 3b, 3c |
| 4 | Group Set-Up | 4a, 4b, 4c, 4d |
| 5 | Teacher Furniture | 5a, 5b, 5c, 5d, 5e |
| 6 | Ancillary | 6a through 6n |
| 7 | Storage | 7a through 7g |

Student Tables
Kit 1a pairs the VS Tano stacking table (four tables, 27 by 26 inches) with four four-leg chairs; its bins match those in Kits 2a and 7a. Kit 1b uses VS Shift+ Thumbprint concave and convex tables, two of each at 21 by 38 inches. Kit 1c uses four VS Lite stacking tables at 21 by 27 inches. Two-top kits are 2a (VS Eco Table, two tables 20 by 52 inches, adjustable 23 to 32 inches), 2b (Fleetwood Plane, two tables 24 by 60 inches, adjustable 23 to 32 inches) and 2c (Fleetwood Plane standing, two tables 24 by 60 inches with foot rail, adjustable 34 to 42 inches, with five-star stools). Four-top kits are 3a (VS Lite, one table 27 by 55 inches), 3b (VS Flip Table RU, one table 27 by 63 inches with markerboard surface, adjustable 29 to 38 inches) and 3c (Fleetwood Plane, one table 36 by 60 inches, adjustable 34 to 42 inches). Four-leg seat heights adjust from 16.5 to 21.5 inches; five-star stool seats from 20.5 to 30.75 inches.

Group, Teacher, Ancillary and Storage
Group set-ups comprise the VS Puzzle table at 65 by 45 inches in seated (4a) and standing/bar (4b) heights, the VS RondoLift 39 by 39 inch square or 39 inch diameter round height-adjustable table (4c), and the VS Base Station semi-circle 30 by 60 inch markerboard table adjustable 23 to 32 inches (4d). Teacher kits 5a through 5d all include a VS EcoTable rectangle table 23 by 55 inches on four casters plus a task chair, varying the storage element (KI Tattoo tower 24 W x 22 D x 46 H; chest 36 W x 18 D x 20-3/8 H; pedestal 12 W x 18 D x 15-7/8 H; VS Homebox 20 W x 35 D x 45 H). Kit 5e is an Ergotron LearnFit mobile desk, 24 by 22 inches, adjustable 29 to 45 inches, with a VS LuPoStool at 24 inch seat height. Ancillary kits cover soft benches, lounge and tablet chairs, a 30 inch diameter markerboard 'sushi' table, an Egan mobile markerboard 36 W x 60 H, rockers and ottomans, leaf-tent retreats, Fomcore nests, floor learning kits, and a 9 foot by 12 foot Lakeshore rug recommended for up to 30 students. Storage kits 7a through 7d are VS Shift+ Transfer units, 42 or 60 inches wide by 17 inches deep by 44 inches high; 7e is a Smith System Cascade two-sided whiteboard unit 43 by 21 by 70 inches; 7f and 7g are Lakeshore Flex-Space shelving and a mobile bin center.
2023_066_5_d_pilot_classroom_furniture_d.verbose:
Item 5.D. for the March 21, 2023 Troy School District Board meeting is a design packet titled 'Pilot Classroom Furniture Design Kits,' dated February 8, 2023 and prepared for the Troy School District.

General information. The packet asks participants for their 'feelings about color,' stating that input will be gathered at Workshop #2 and factored into final color selections with the Executive team. The professional team and executive team will size furniture according to grade level, with typical height bands of Pre-K, Pre-K to K, K to 2nd, 3rd to 5th, 3rd to 12th, and 9th to 12th, and dedicated height guidance for K to 2nd grade and 3rd to 12th grade classrooms. Kits include opportunities for individual, two-person and four-person seating. Most present Mobility Option A and Mobility Option B, with chair styles of Four Leg with Glides (K to 1st grade option), Four Leg plus Casters (K to 12 option), and Five-Star plus Casters; four-leg seat heights adjust from 16.5 inches to 21.5 inches and five-star stool seat heights from 20.5 inches to 30.75 inches.

Single student tables. Kit 1a is the VS Tano Stacking Table, an asymmetrical polygon, including four tables 27 inches by 26 inches, fixed height, stacking, two glides plus two casters, and four four-leg chairs with glides; tables stack without bins in place, and its bins are the same as those in Kit 2a and can be used with Kit 7a. Kit 1b is the VS Shift + Thumbprint Stacking Table (concave plus convex): two convex tables 21 inches by 38 inches and two concave tables 21 inches by 38 inches, fixed height, stacking, two glides plus two casters, with four four-leg chairs with glides; it shares a radius with Group Set-Up Kit 4d and Ancillary Kit 6b and is described as the largest of the single student tables. Kit 1c is the VS Lite Stacking Table (rectangle) with four tables 21 inches by 27 inches, fixed height, stacking, two glides plus two casters, and four four-leg chairs; each table is 27 inches wide, so two equal the width of one Kit 3a table.

Two-top student tables. Kit 2a is the VS Eco Table, a rectangle, with two tables 20 inches by 52 inches, height-adjustable from 23 inches to 32 inches with two glides plus two casters, and four four-leg chairs with glides; a backpack hook is shown and the 'Set It & Forget It' legs adjust with a small tool. Kit 2b is the Fleetwood Plane Unitized Frame Table with two tables 24 inches by 60 inches on four casters, height-adjustable 23 inches to 32 inches, and four four-leg chairs; possible additions are a table shelf and backpack hook, with Kit 6c cross-referenced for a lounge concept using Mobility Option B. Kit 2c is the standing version: two Fleetwood Plane tables 24 inches by 60 inches with four casters and a foot rail, height-adjustable 34 inches to 42 inches, with four height-adjustable five-star stools.

Four-top student tables. Kit 3a is the VS Lite Stacking Table: one table 27 inches by 55 inches, fixed height, stacking, two glides plus two casters, with four four-leg chairs; at 55 inches wide it equals two Kit 1c tables. Kit 3b is the VS Flip Table RU: one table 27 inches by 63 inches with four casters, flip top and markerboard surface, height-adjustable 29 inches to 38 inches, with four five-star stools; flipped vertically it acts as a markerboard and multiples nest together. Kit 3c is the Fleetwood Plane table: one table 36 inches by 60 inches with four casters, foot rail, height-adjustable 34 inches to 42 inches, meeting counter height (34 to 36 inches) or bar height (42 inches), with four five-star stools.

Group set-ups. These accommodate groups of four comfortably and may accommodate up to six, and were designed with guided instruction in mind. Kit 4a is the VS Puzzle Table at seated fixed height, one table 65 inches by 45 inches on four casters with four rocking stools; one table can seat three to six students and the tables intentionally fit together. Kit 4b is the same 65 inch by 45 inch Puzzle top at standing (fixed) bar height on four casters with four adjustable-height five-star stools. Kit 4c is the VS RondoLift, either one 39 inch by 39 inch square or one 39 inch diameter round height-adjustable table on casters, with four rocking stools, using on-demand lever height adjustment. Kit 4d is the VS Base Station semi-circle: one table 30 inches by 60 inches, height-adjustable 23 inches to 32 inches, with casters and markerboard surface, plus four rocking stools; it comfortably seats four and fits within a group of Thumbprint tables from Kit 1b. Stacking Stool A and Stacking Stool B are noted as available only in 18 inch height, best for 5th grade plus secondary.

Teacher furniture. The stated concept is a 'deconstructed' teacher station separating work surface from storage. Kits 5a, 5b, 5c and 5d each include one VS EcoTable rectangle table 23 inches by 55 inches with four casters at fixed seated height and one teacher task chair, differing in storage: 5a adds a locking KI Tattoo storage tower on casters, 24 inches W by 22 inches D by 46 inches H, just under 4 feet tall and able to hold a short coat; 5b adds a locking KI Tattoo storage chest on casters with an upholstered seating pad, 36 inches W by 18 inches D by 20-3/8 inches H; 5c adds a locking KI Tattoo pedestal on casters with pencil drawer and file storage inside, 12 inches W by 18 inches D by 15-7/8 inches H, which fits under the table; and 5d adds a VS Homebox pull-out locking storage unit, 20 inches W by 35 inches D by 45 inches H, whose total depth when pulled out is 5 feet 2 inches. Kit 5e, 'Perch,' is an Ergotron LearnFit mobile desk 24 inches by 22 inches, height-adjustable 29 inches to 45 inches with bag hook and accessory bin, paired with a VS LuPoStool with back at a fixed 24 inch seat height, described as a true sit-to-stand desk that would also work for students.

Ancillary kits. Kit 6a (VS Shift+ Landscape) includes two soft rectangle benches 41 inches by 20 inches at 15 inches high and one soft cube 20 inches by 20 inches at 15 inches high, usable with Kit 2a tables and around a floor rug. Kit 6b includes two soft arc benches 43 inches by 20 inches at 15 inches high, which fit the curve of the Kit 7b storage units and pair with Kit 1b tables. Kit 6c (KI MyPlace Lounge) includes two armless sofas with 32 inch high low back at 48 inches W by 26 inches D, one armless lounge chair with 32 inch high low back at 26 inches W by 26 inches D, and two laptop tables with 20 inch by 26 inch work surfaces at 26 inches W by 20 inches D by 26 inches H. Kit 6d (Integra Coffee House Tablet Lounge) includes one 'standard' size lounge chair with integral tablet arm rated up to 300 lbs; standard size is 22-1/2 inches wide with 18 inch seat height, an 18 inch W by 12 inch D tablet and casters, while the 'kids' size deduct option is 20 inches wide with 16 inch seat height, a 13 inch diameter tablet and legs with glides. Kit 6e, the 'sushi set-up,' pairs one Fleetwood round table 30 inches in diameter at 20 inches high with markerboard top and two rocking stools at 12 inches high. Kit 6f (Egan V-Series Mobile) is one mobile markerboard with magnetic grip rail and magnets, 36 inches W by 60 inches H. Kit 6g combines two Smith System Flowform upholstered rocker chairs, 26-1/4 inches D by 20-1/2 inches W by 25.5 inches H, with two Fomcore log ottomans, 17 inches L by 15 inches W by 18 inches H, the rocker provided in kids size for elementary and XL size for secondary. Kit 6h (VS America Shift+ Landscape + Leaf) includes six leaf tents, six curved padded floor mats 41 inches by 34 inches, one pole and one drum table with integrated storage. Kit 6i includes two leaf tents and two square floor mats 41 inches by 33 inches, attachable to the backside of storage Kits 7a, 7b, 7c or 7d. Kit 6j (Fomcore Nest Series) includes one Robin's Nest with pad, 45 inches L by 21 inches W by 39 inches H, compared against the Eagle's Nest at 57 inches L by 24 inches W by 51 inches. Kit 6k includes two Lakeshore Learning lap desks and two position chairs with adjustable back rests. Kit 6l is one Lakeshore Learning area rug, 9 feet by 12 feet, in style A, B, C or D, recommended for up to 30 students. Kit 6m is one Sauder Education Trey convertible chair, including both the seat and the base/table. Kit 6n is one set of four Lakeshore Learning Flex-Space comfy nesting benches.

Storage kits. Kits 7a, 7b, 7c and 7d are VS Shift+ Transfer Storage units with push handles, locking casters and two side magnets that link units, and perforated magnetic metal backs. Kit 7a is a one-sided mobile storage unit with bins, 42 inches wide by 17 inches deep by 44 inches high, configurable with thirty 3 inch bins, fifteen 6 inch bins, or a combination, its bins matching those at Kits 1a and 2a. Kit 7b is a one-sided curved mobile unit with open shelves, 60 inches wide by 17 inches deep by 44 inches high, working with Kits 6b, 1b and 4b. Kit 7c is a one-sided mobile unit with open shelves, 42 inches wide by 17 inches deep by 44 inches high. Kit 7d is a one-sided locking mobile cabinet with doors, 42 inches wide by 17 inches deep by 44 inches high. Kit 7e is a Smith System Cascade two-sided whiteboard unit, 43 inches wide by 21 inches deep by 70 inches high, configurable with thirty 3 inch bins or fourteen 6 inch bins, with totes 16-5/8 inches D by 18-3/8 inches W that do not cross over to other furniture. Kit 7f (Lakeshore Learning Flex-Space All-Purpose Storage) includes two one-sided open shelving units with two shelves, shown at 36 inches wide by 14.5 inches deep by 46 inches high and 36 inches wide by 14.5 inches deep by 32 inches high, with each shelf holding about 36 books, the two-shelf unit about 72 books and the three-shelf unit about 108 books. Kit 7g is a Lakeshore Learning Flex-Space Mobile Storage Bin Center, 23 inches wide by 14.5 inches deep by 34 inches high, with twelve tall bins included. The packet ends with the line 'You are a Designer!'

2023_067_troy_middle_school_learning_eco.paragraph: A Fielding International 'Learning Ecosystem Report' for the Troy School District, presented at the March 7, 2023 Board of Education meeting alongside the Discovery Report. It records the mission themes staff and students identified for a re-imagined middle school, the results of a design-pattern voting exercise in which Learning Community drew the most votes at 24, and prototype core learning layouts with typical area sizes such as an 800 sf Learning Studio and a 980 sf Science Lab. It closes with a six-block daily framework beginning at 8:00 AM and ending at 3:35 PM.
2023_067_troy_middle_school_learning_eco.page:
Middle School Mission
The report asks what the mission of a re-imagined middle school experience might be and lists seven answers: (1) Provide Experiential and Authentic Learning; (2) Strive for Engagement and Fun; (3) Foster Cultural Competencies; (4) Promote Social Emotional Learning & Empathy; (5) Cultivate Future-Ready Skills; (6) Build Relationships & Community and Connectedness; (7) Encourage Healthy Risks. Each is expanded in a Students-versus-Staff table answering 'What does this mean?', 'What would we hear or see?' and 'What would it feel like?'

Time, Space, and Technology
Time ideas include morning advisory as the heart of school culture, recess and extended lunch, flexible blocks of time, common planning time, student-led learning opportunities (Genius Hour), late-start or early-release options, and exploring a modified block schedule with a 'skinny' day. Technology ideas include engaging learning management systems, a more interoperable data platform, more adaptive assessments, engaging students in review of performance data, more simulation and modeling experiences, and using technology only when required rather than by default. Space ideas include multi-purpose flexible spaces, healthy school designs promoting wellness, comfortable at-home conditions, stronger outdoor connections, greater variability and variety of spaces, and natural lighting and transparency.

Design Pattern Voting
Participants placed dots on the design patterns that most excited them for the future of teaching and learning.
| Rank | Pattern | Votes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Learning Community | 24 |
| 2 | Transparency | 20 |
| 3 | Learning Commons | 18 |
| 4 | Variable Seating | 18 |
| 5 | Indoor-Outdoor Connections | 16 |

The Top 15 list continues with 6 Teacher Collaboration, 7 Daylighting, 8 STEAM Workshop, 9 Small Group Room, 10 Casual Eating Area, 11 Calming Retreat, 12 Integrating the Arts & Performance, 13 Neighborhood as a School, 14 Outdoor Classroom, and 15 Active Hallway. A 'Key Design Patterns' section then presents each of the fifteen in turn.

The Ideal Learning Ecosystem
Three plan diagrams, Core Learning Concept Layout 1, Core Learning Concept Layout 2 and Core Learning Layout 3, arrange learning studios, a science lab, production commons, restoration and research commons with a research cave, special education and sensory space, teacher workshop, small group rooms (SGR), storage and restrooms. All three list the same typical areas.
| Space | Typical Area |
| --- | --- |
| Learning Studio | 800 sf |
| Science Lab | 980 sf |
| Production Commons | 800 sf |
| Special Education & Sensory | 600 sf |
| Restoration & Research Commons | 500 sf |
| Teacher Workshop | 350 sf |
| Small Group Room | 100 sf |
| Storage | 100 sf |

Day in the Life Blocks
The closing section walks the core plan through six blocks, each captioned with student and instructor activity precedents and a narrative: Block 1, 8:00 - 9:00 AM; Block 2, 9:05 - 10:35 AM; Block 3, 10:40 - 11:40 am; Block 4, 11:45 - 1:15 PM; Block 5, 1:20 - 2:20 PM; Block 6, 2:25 - 3:35 PM.
2023_067_troy_middle_school_learning_eco.verbose:
The Troy School District Learning Ecosystem Report was prepared by Fielding International, whose tagline reads 'Designing schools where learners thrive,' and appeared on the March 7, 2023 Board of Education agenda as a companion to the Troy Middle School Discovery Report. Its running footer identifies it with the Troy School District Discovery Report series.

Middle School Mission. The report asks 'What might be the mission of a re-imagined Middle School experience?' and answers with seven numbered themes: 1. Provide Experiential and Authentic Learning; 2. Strive for Engagement and Fun; 3. Foster Cultural Competencies; 4. Promote Social Emotional Learning & Empathy; 5. Cultivate Future-Ready Skills; 6. Build Relationships & Community and Connectedness; 7. Encourage Healthy Risks. Each theme receives a page comparing Student and Staff responses to three questions: what does this mean, what would we hear or see, and what would it feel like.

Experiential and authentic learning. Students defined it as learning that relates to the outside world, field trips and guest speakers, and becoming the expert; staff as stepping away from lecture, simulation experiences and flexibility in assessment. Students expected to see peer-to-peer communication, engaged learning and curiosity; staff described the teacher as 'guide on the side.' Students said it would feel liberating and provide ownership and value; staff anticipated potential stress from planning and coordination alongside being impressed with student achievements.

Engagement and fun. Students described a 'menu' of options, choice plus voice, hands-on activities, a lessened homework load, field trips and project-based learning. Staff described creating authentic problem- or project-based learning experiences focused on student voice and choice, connecting interdisciplinary work leading to empowerment as an adult, analytical skills and higher-order thinking, and being well rounded. Observable indicators included respect, joy, fun, games, laughing and hands-on activities for students, and 'organized chaos' with non-traditional deliverable outcomes, changing assessments, teacher as partnership, coach or mentor, and teaching models, structures and their applications for staff. Feelings ranged from fun, motivation, welcoming, 'be yourself' and 'challenge yourself' to a slightly more anxious environment requiring growth and process.

Cultural competencies. Students sought exposure to various cultures, representation in the curriculum and in images in the building, understanding of self and others, welcoming and better learning environments; staff sought a responsive approach to student culture, more diverse alignment of staff, culturally responsive teaching and a stronger understanding of their students. Indicators included working in diverse groupings and collaboration, healthy discourse, students experiencing different cultures and thought early on, differentiated learning for heterogeneous groups, staff better supporting students to increase empathy, and elevating student voice. Feelings included being seen, increased sense of belonging, safe and inclusive environments, a higher sense of community, being valued, empathy, an 'ALL means ALL' approach to planning and problem solving, more informed decisions about students, connection, and greater relational capacity.

Social emotional learning and empathy. Students wanted an environment where they feel safe and ready to learn, opportunities to explore other points of view, explicitly taught character traits and values, and strategies including mindfulness; staff wanted proper training, research-based support, opportunities to explore, communication and quick staff check-ins. Visible indicators included adults and professionals on hand to talk to, community in classrooms, safety protocols, a common language of respect, spaces dedicated to specific purposes or needs, and 'recess' time, plus more schedule time to build relationships with other staff and students, acknowledgement from peers and administration, and coworkers to talk to. Feelings listed were inclusive, welcoming, supported, refreshed, safe, valued, connected, relieved, 'take a few,' and seen or heard.

Future-ready skills. Students described trying new things, stretching one's self, knowing ways and strategies for learning, fewer siloed learning experiences and process over product; staff described changes in assessment practices, time and practice and hope in teacher growth, cross-curricular ownership of teaching, professional learning on how to foster the skills, and evidence plus concrete measures. Indicators included creativity, voices, engaged autonomy, self-reflection on learning, growth in these skills, variety in output or product, learning from each other, naming skills and goals in development, hosting reflective conversation, trying and risk, and conversation between teachers. Feelings included more autonomy and choice every day, authenticity, ownership and pride, treating a different place, rate or age as normal, uncertainty, a less linear path, and feeling valued in adult growth, united, meaningful, valuable and significant.

Relationships, community and connectedness. Students said it means feeling part of a community, feeling welcomed and appreciated, connecting with the community and helping with risk-taking; staff said feeling appreciated and welcomed, enhancing and optimizing leadership skills, and feeling part of a community. Indicators included identifying a trusted adult, respect for all people, different people feeling more comfortable to share openly about who they are, seeing and hearing school spirit with increased participation, more teamwork rather than individual opinions, and more buy-in. Feelings included feeling more free, open, authentic and less stressed, being more invested rather than seeing school as a waste of time, increased pride in school and selves, being more academically accomplished, happy teachers, easier communication, job satisfaction and openness to change.

Healthy risks. Students described more opportunities and choice, multiple ways to show learning understanding, and productive struggle; staff described moving away from 'right' answers, process over product, different students shining, changing mindset, being not the expert but the ultimate cheerleader, and progress-based grading. Phrases expected included 'Let's give this a try,' 'You will be graded on progress' and 'Yet,' alongside staff questions about grades, high school and parents, and new teaching pedagogy. Other indicators were intentional discussions, all different responses, vulnerability and choice in seating. Feelings included supported, safe, fun and engaging, liberating, less stressful, comfortable spaces, safety with parents and evaluation, and an acknowledgment that change can be uncomfortable.

Time, technology and space. Under 'How Might we Use Time Differently?' the report lists morning advisory as the heart of school culture, recess and extended lunch, flexible blocks of time to create conditions for new opportunities, creating common planning time, scheduling student-led learning opportunities (Genius Hour), considering late-start or early release opportunities, and exploring a modified block schedule with a 'skinny' day. Under technology it lists exploring engaging learning management systems, adopting a more interoperable data platform, using more adaptive assessments, engaging students in review of performance data, increasing access to simulation and modeling experiences, and using technology only when required instead of as the default in order to create balance. Under space it lists ensuring spaces have multiple purposes and can be used flexibly, placing emphasis on healthy school designs that promote wellness, creating comfortable conditions so students feel more at home, strengthening outdoor connections, increasing the variability and variety of spaces, and treating natural lighting and transparency as critical for fostering connections and allowing student-led learning.

Design patterns. In a dot-voting exercise described as 'Connecting the Dots with Design Patterns,' participants marked the design patterns that most excited them. The top five, in order, were Learning Community with 24 votes, Transparency with 20 votes, Learning Commons with 18 votes, Variable Seating with 18 votes, and Indoor-Outdoor Connections with 16 votes. The Top 15 list continues with 6 Teacher Collaboration, 7 Daylighting, 8 STEAM Workshop, 9 Small Group Room, 10 Casual Eating Area, 11 Calming Retreat, 12 Integrating the Arts & Performance, 13 Neighborhood as a school, 14 Outdoor Classroom, and 15 Active Hallway. A subsequent 'Key Design Patterns' sequence devotes a page to each: 1. Learning Community, 2. Transparency, 3. Learning Commons, 4. Variable Seating, 5. Indoor-Outdoor Connections, 6. Teacher Collaboration Room, 7. Daylighting, 8. STEAM Workshop, 9. Small Group Room, 10. Casual Eating Areas, 11. Calming Retreat, 12. Integrated Arts & Performance, 13. Neighborhood as School, 14. Outdoor Classroom, and 15. Active Hallway.

The ideal learning ecosystem. Three plan diagrams, labeled Core Learning Concept Layout 1, Core Learning Concept Layout 2 and Core Learning Layout 3, arrange multiple learning studios, a science lab, production commons, a restoration and research commons including a research cave, special education and sensory space, a teacher workshop, small group rooms (SGR), storage (STRG, STG, STR) and restrooms around a shared core. All three layouts list the same typical areas: Learning Studio 800 sf, Science Lab 980 sf, Production Commons 800 sf, Special Education & Sensory 600 sf, Restoration & Research Commons 500 sf, Teacher Workshop 350 sf, Small Group Room 100 sf, and Storage 100 sf.

Day in the life. The final section repeats the core plan across six time blocks, each captioned with 'Student Activity Precedent,' 'Instructor Activity Precedent' and 'Narrative': Block 1 from 8:00 to 9:00 AM; Block 2 from 9:05 to 10:35 AM; Block 3 from 10:40 to 11:40 am; Block 4 from 11:45 to 1:15 PM; Block 5 from 1:20 to 2:20 PM; and Block 6 from 2:25 to 3:35 PM.

2023_068_troy_middle_school_discovery_re.paragraph: A Fielding International Discovery Report for the Troy School District, presented at the March 7, 2023 Board of Education meeting, documenting visioning work for the district's middle schools. It compiles leader priorities, six vision statements, observed environmental and program challenges, snapshots of Baker, Boulan Park, Smith and Boyd R. Larson middle schools, and summaries of conversations with teachers and students. A two-day visioning workshop produced rankings of teaching modalities, with inquiry-based rated most familiar at 2.4 and competency-based least familiar at 5.5, plus brain-science responses and a participant-designed sample schedule running from 8:00 am to 3:03 pm.
2023_068_troy_middle_school_discovery_re.page:
Scope
Fielding International's Discovery Report for the Troy School District covers visioning, observations of existing middle school environments and programs, teacher and student conversations, and a two-day visioning workshop.

Visioning and Vision Statements
Future priorities of Troy leaders are grouped under pillars including Early Childhood to Career, Equity and Well-Being, Deep Learning, and Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families, with priorities such as student driven learning, a schedule that resembles a modern workplace, programs accessible to all students, connection and pride, fresh learning spaces, natural light, collaboration to solve meaningful problems, room to adapt, high levels of student achievement and authentic measures, increased student/teacher collaboration, and families visiting schools to observe program. Six vision statements are listed: innovative uses of space and technology that can adapt to future program; a student sense of belonging and pride inspired by meaningful relationships; students as agents of their own learning; the practice and understanding of collaboration between students, teachers and community; consistently improved teaching and learning; and whole child wellness at the center.

Observed Challenges
Environmental challenges: technology accumulated in single rooms, inflexible furniture limiting agility, lack of natural or controllable lighting, rigid cafeteria design, underutilized media centers, hallways used for breakout with no informal student spaces, and limited space for individual projects and learning support. Program challenges: technology use often mimicking traditional strategies, classroom features limiting experience variety, challenging outdoor connections, 'templated' activities limiting autonomy, voice and choice, and large group instruction far more prevalent than other strategies. Snapshots in time were taken at Baker Middle School, Boulan Park Middle School, Smith Middle School and Boyd R. Larson Middle School.

What Was Heard
Teachers reported that collaboration is situational and informal, occurring in hallways and before or after school, that the schedule does not allow shared planning time, that there is little collective understanding of the 6 C's beyond the online platform, and that technology use largely augments or replaces analog tools, with all examples falling in the Augmentation band of SAMR. Students said they do not really know whether teachers work together, cited math, science and elective projects as challenging in a good way, and named friends, electives and PE among the best parts of the day. Requested changes included recess, longer passing time, later start time, bigger lockers, and better bathrooms, gym and food.

Workshop Findings
Participants ranked teaching modalities from most to least known: Inquiry-based (2.4), Project-based (2.6), Flexibility (3.5), Personalized (4), Voice + Choice (4.6), Interdisciplinary (5.1), Competency-based (5.5). They responded to brain-science statements drawn from the World Economic Forum, the National Institute of Mental Health, the UCLA Center for the Developing Adolescent and Nature. A Keep / Discard / Evolve exercise kept portfolios, Genius Hour, relationships and project-based learning; discarded the current grading system, bells, walls, homework, desks and tracking; and evolved learning spaces and time, feedback and assessments, and competency-based and interdisciplinary learning. A 'Day-in-the-Life' charette produced a sample schedule with a start time of 8:00 am and an end time of 3:03 pm across seven hours, beginning with Architectural Science and Algebra 1.
2023_068_troy_middle_school_discovery_re.verbose:
The Troy School District Discovery Report, prepared by Fielding International, appears on the March 7, 2023 Board of Education agenda. Its footer reads 'Fielding International / Designing schools where learners thrive - Troy School District / Discovery Report.'

Visioning. Future priorities of Troy leaders are mapped to pillars: Early Childhood to Career (student driven learning; schedule that resembles a modern workplace; programs accessible to all students); Equity and Well-Being (connection and pride; fresh learning spaces; natural light); Deep Learning (collaboration to solve meaningful problems; room to adapt; high levels of student achievement and authentic measures); and Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families (increase student/teacher collaboration; families visiting schools to observe program). 'How we get there' lists student voice included, clearly defined goals, community involvement, equity and inclusion, a collective vision of what could be, excitement, and shifts in pedagogy. Six numbered vision statements answer 'Who do we want to be?': innovative uses of space and technology that can adapt to future program; a student sense of belonging and pride inspired by meaningful relationships; students as agents of their own learning; the practice and understanding of collaboration between students, teachers and community; consistently improved teaching and learning; and whole child wellness at the center.

Challenges in the observed environment. Listed conditions are technology accumulated in single rooms and less integrated; inflexible furniture limiting agility; lack of natural and/or controllable lighting; rigid cafeteria design limiting utilization and use options; underutilized media centers; hallways used for breakout with no informal spaces for students; and limited space for individual projects and learning support.

Challenges in the observed program. Listed conditions are technology use often mimicking traditional strategies; classroom features limiting experience variety; challenging outdoor connections that may limit use; 'templated' activities limiting autonomy, voice and choice; and large group instruction far more prevalent compared to other strategies.

Snapshots in time. Photo sections document Baker Middle School, Boulan Park Middle School, Smith Middle School and Boyd R. Larson Middle School.

What we heard from teachers. On collaboration, notes record that teachers fit collaboration into their schedules as needed, so it occurs informally in hallways, in each other's rooms and before or after school; that working together is incidental rather than planned and happens mostly within a department rather than by grade level; and that the schedule does not allow for shared planning time. On the 6 C's, a teacher response of 'Not by categories, we do benchmark assessments in math and English' is cited as suggesting a lack of understanding of the 6 Cs, with teachers otherwise pointing only to notes in the online learning platform and no evidence of a shared understanding of what good collaboration looks like or how to teach collaboration skills explicitly. On technology for transformation, the note 'Using the iPads means we can do a lot more' is qualified by the observation that all examples given were in the Augmentation band of SAMR, and that the tech teacher did not seem familiar with the SAMR model. The teacher conversations summary concludes that collaboration is highly situational and informal rather than part of routine or structure; that many describe it as sharing ideas instead of working alongside others; that collaborative tools are used but not frequently; that inadequate shared planning time and schedule are frequently cited barriers; that there is little coherence or collective understanding of the 6 C's, though some teachers described positive movement toward inquiry-based learning, multiple teachers indicated all exposure came from the online platform, and COVID impacts may have disrupted prior work; and that technology use mostly augments or replaces older analog tools, with few examples of technology as an authoring tool and limits in access to software and training.

What we heard from students. Asked how they know teachers work together, students offered 'I see them sitting together, but don't know if they are working or just hanging out,' 'Not from different subjects, only the same subject,' and 'When one teacher doesn't know an answer, they ask another teacher.' Challenging tasks named included a book club on a hard book, science lab, unit enrichment activities, science quizzes, making a WordPress website, making bread in life skills, a social studies chariot design, an advertising project arguing for the 'Best Era,' and math that is 'really challenging in a good way.' What students love included nice and funny teachers, a kind community, friends, little bullying, electives, and 'I don't know, it just feels like home.' Best parts of the day included friends, clean hallways, science, social studies, math, PE 'because I can move around,' health class, little rooms to study, life skills, lunch, choir, video tech, ELA and passing time. 'Magic wants' included recess, a place to play volleyball, longer passing time, bigger lockers, nicer bathrooms, phones at passing time and lunch, more understanding about late work, shorter hours, more after-school activities, a longer basketball season, fixing the track, a fun library, going outside more, no homework, a new school color, a later start time, more gym space, soccer goals, comfy chairs, free lunch again, bigger rooms, better food and more club choices. The summary reports that students really do not know if teachers work together, with common responses about teachers dropping into another class to ask a quick question and one student mentioning the 'collaboration room'; that challenging tasks are mostly attributed to math, science and electives and usually have more than one solution; and that students love their community, feel safe, feel they belong and feel teachers care. Ranked best parts of the day: 1 anytime with friends, 2 sports and physical education, 3 electives, 4 various other subjects. Ranked changes: 1 more time with friends, 2 longer passing times and later start times, 3 upgraded facilities for school, sports and food, 4 going outside more, 5 no homework.

Other observations and reactions. Flexible furniture is in high demand; collaboration is not the norm because conditions make it challenging; students are generally happy; building facility and schedule are barriers to innovation; shared spaces like the media center could be utilized more; many 'cookie cutter' tasks including coloring worksheets were observed especially in the sciences; windowless rooms are prevalent and problematic; positive teaching experiences are isolated and teacher dependent although relationships are high quality; and students have little time outside lunch and passing time to just be kids, reflect and build relationships.

Visioning Workshop, Day 1. Initial reactions asked whether students love the teachers but are bored in classes, and noted student desire for more collaboration and social interaction, that outside spaces and spaces for movement and eating are as important as academic spaces, that participants learn the same amount with and without homework, that flexible furniture is in high demand but only useful if teachers know how to use it, that media centers could be collaborative spaces, that students need breaks from thinking constantly, and that there needs to be more student agency, creativity and innovation. Reactions to building 'snapshots' included better utilization of space, whether dedicated classroom spaces are needed for all or could be shared, that all snapshots look the same, lots of sitting with little for kinesthetic learners, the need for wall space utilization and vertical non-permanent workspaces, an aesthetic that feels unwelcoming and dated, teachers at the front controlling the goals, and 'So many rows!' Reflections on school images raised cafeteria accessibility, the uselessness of outside space without 'tools' that promote socializing and learning, the need for common teacher workspaces, more sunlight, more collaborative student spaces, technology disconnected from daily use, re-examining the traditional media center as structured for adult learners, more equitable spaces, and pride in teachers being creative with limited resources. On technology's future impact, participants noted that access to answers can be helpful support and a harmful crutch, that technology lets teachers and students learn from each other and lets students practice teaching and leadership, that tools expand thinking, and the need to create, use and understand the impact of AI (user to author). Surfacing themes included lack of autonomy and choice, opportunity for differentiation, many rules, kids trapped, school confined by structure and schedule, a risk-averse system stifling creativity, and planning for the unknown. Conditions to create in the new school included student choice, students and teachers learning together, flexible spaces and furniture, technology fitting student needs, outdoor connections, collaborative opportunities, focus on skills, less stressful classes, inspiring electives, welcoming spaces, relationship building and social emotional learning. An 'Important, Best, Excited' exercise named flexibility, collaboration, accessibility, community, student choice, safety, better use of space and choosing growth over grades as most important; small school size, variety, exposure, willingness to try new things, community and family support, clubs and activities, teacher autonomy and relationships as what Troy does best; and natural light, flexible seating, making DEI common practice, deepening community ties, real change and disruption, being a model for other schools, de-siloed classes, student-led learning and more schedule flexibility as sources of excitement. Questions included how pedagogy will change after the environment changes, whether there will be more collaborative spaces throughout Troy schools, whether big organizational structures can change while maintaining the best parts, how to get over a fear of failure, and how to bring more natural light to all spaces. Opportunities included surveying stakeholders, rethinking media spaces and unused space, and incorporating kids being kids, more extracurriculars and more choice based on student interest.

Visioning Workshop, Day 2. Participants ranked a list of teaching modalities by what they know most and least about, producing Inquiry-based (2.4), Project-based (2.6), Flexibility (3.5), Personalized (4), Voice + Choice (4.6), Interdisciplinary (5.1) and Competency-based (5.5). Participants then read statements about child brain development and learning from the World Economic Forum, the National Institute of Mental Health, the UCLA Center for the Developing Adolescent, and Nature, and commented on stickies. 'Adolescents are highly sensitive to respect' drew responses on relationship building, positive feedback and a student-driven definition of respect. 'Adolescents are drawn to novel experiences' drew innovative teaching techniques, community partnerships, flexible space, embedded social emotional learning and student choice. 'Scientists have discovered that IQ can increase significantly during the teenage years' drew more positive feedback, more opportunities, more pathways and reduced tracking. 'Witnessing traumatic events can have an impact on the physical development of a child's brain' drew more counselors, trauma informed pedagogy training, schedule time for check-ins and relationship building. 'Teens need more sleep than children and adults' drew a later start, shorter school days, less homework and time and space to rest at school. 'Adolescence is a critical time for brain development' drew student choice, passion projects, flexible scheduling, community connections and relevant curriculum. 'Teen brains may be more vulnerable to stress' drew coping skills, mindfulness, time outside and connection with nature, embedded social emotional learning, breaks in the day, and limiting homework, grades and tests in favor of positive feedback and portfolios. Team research posters on effective ways to learn produced common themes of more opportunity and choice, self monitoring, interleaving and spiral curriculum, more immediate feedback, real world connections, a Goldilocks challenge level, students teaching peers, learning from mistakes, hands-on movement and fun, and collaboration.

The 21st-century learner. Participants characterized the learner as tech savvy, consumers and creators of media, creative and smart, knowing more than teachers think they do, and fast learners; supports listed were multi-use space, a comfortable environment with diverse options, teachers as guides, students following their interests, more movement, respect and trust, fewer tests and less homework, and focus on skills and engagement. Alignment ideas included schedule changes such as a shorter week, later start time and more rest time; student-centered learning; rethinking grades, tests and homework; cooperative and innovative teaching including project-based learning; relationship and respect building; outside time and connection with nature; social emotional learning and mental health; and space and time for play, movement and creativity.

Challenges and affordances. Affordances included students being more focused and engaged, more understanding and respect, increased fulfillment, classroom management allowing more one-to-one time, the teacher's purpose changing to mentor, alleviated stress, more satisfied and motivated students, students feeling understood and that learning is relevant, students owning their learning, seeing adults model discomfort, less stress from tests, homework and grades, and a healthier environment. Challenges included teachers giving up ownership of student learning, a shift in the identity of a teacher, ambiguity, being vulnerable in front of students, change being hard and more work, students being harder to control, disengaged students, organization and schedule change, teaching critical thinking and perseverance instead of facts, consistency across teachers and standards, new community relationships, too many choices, lack of life experiences, students needing structure or help with choices, project fatigue, and difficulty establishing new routines.

Setting the dials for the future. The Keep / Discard / Evolve exercise kept portfolio, Genius Hour, relationships, student voice and choice, Celebration of Learning, project based learning, passion projects, feedback, high expectation, real world experiences, and focus on student equity and well being. It discarded the current grading system, bells, walls, short lunch, passing time and early start, rigidity of space and schedule, unnatural lighting, constant instruction, one size fits all assessment, lecture, homework, desks, tracking, unhealthy food and busy work. It evolved learning spaces and time, passion projects, feedback and assessments, mindset on student ability, food, comfort, fun, project based learning, student voice and choice, creative time, community partnerships, inquiry, teaching styles, competency based learning, interdisciplinary learning, real world and career connections, student teaching, and teacher professional development.

Day-in-the-Life charette. Participants designed a day in the new middle school with a start time of 8:00 am and an end time of 3:03 pm: Hour 1 Architectural Science, Hour 2 Algebra 1, Hour 3 Archery (Electives), Hour 4 Creative Period, Hour 5 World History, Hour 6 P.E., Hour 7 English. Students would choose one course from each category: Science (Chemistry, Architectural Science, Reproduction Science, Material Science); Social Studies (World History, Social World); Phys Ed (Phys Ed, Archery, Track, Basketball, Baseball/Softball, Net Sports); Math (Geometry, Algebra, Common Maths, Equations); ELA (Reading, Writing, Spelling, Grammar); and Electives (Orchestra, Band, Choir, Art, Digital Apps). System features included one hour a day of creative time with independent choice, students selecting all of their classes, guidelines for assignments, less pressure for grades, options for each class, different ways of teaching, project presentations at the end of each quarter, Monday and Friday time for a personal project, and teachers as guiders. Architectural ideas included collaborative spaces, ranges of seating, hallway seating, windows, maker spaces, movable walls and a student lounge. Stated trade-offs were lots of class options, some work could not be finished, and not all common class information could be given. The closing reflection, under the prompt 'What's the one big thing we need to consider?', listed exciting structure changes in time, scheduling and space, the power of relationships, different teaching modalities, student voice and choice, remembering the brain science, and what this looks like in action.
